content: The Ukrainian Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) refuge is one of the hypothesized areas where human populations sought shelter from the harsh glacial climate approximately 13,000 years ago. This refuge is believed to have been located around the Black Sea region. From this and other LGM refuges, it is theorized that post-glacial recolonization of Europe and Central Asia occurred. The area is thought to have been particularly attractive due to its relatively favorable thermal conditions during the LGM. During the LGM, the European climate was extremely arid. Northern rivers did not carry water as their sources were frozen in glaciers, and sea levels were significantly lower. The Black Sea itself may have experienced substantial evaporation. The temperature at the bottom of the Black Sea is estimated to have been approximately 12°C warmer than at sea level, making it a potentially habitable zone during this period. Haplogroup M17, also known as Hg R1a1, is considered a genetic marker for populations originating from this glacial refuge. This haplogroup, with an inferred age of approximately 15,000 years, is found at high frequencies in regions such as Poland, Russia, Ukraine, the Czech Republic, the Slovak Republic, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. It is also common throughout Central Asia but is rare in East Asia and Western Europe. The microsatellite diversity of R1a1 is thought to be associated with population expansions that occurred after the LGM. This genetic marker has been linked to more recent migrations of Indo-European-speaking peoples from the steppes, spreading the gene to new regions and contributing to its ethnic distribution. This evidence supports the hypothesis that M17 is a diagnostic marker for Indo-Iranian populations. To the northwest, this gene spread into Scandinavian territories and is considered a marker of Viking movements between 800 and 1300 AD. To the east, the gene extended as far as Eastern Siberia, with significant concentrations in Kamchatka and Chukotka. It is even possible that this gene entered the Americas via this route. The current distribution of the M17 (Hg R1a1) marker is characterized by high concentrations across a wide geographic area, from Lapland to Ukraine and from Poland to Kazakhstan and Pakistan. However, there are sharp declines in frequency at the peripheries, likely due to natural barriers or the expansion of populations originating from other LGM refuges, such as those in Spain and the Balkans. Exceptionally high frequencies of R1a1 are observed in populations such as the Kyrgyz, Tajik/Khojant, and Ishkashim, likely due to genetic drift. In contrast, lower concentrations in other regions may be partially attributed to documented intrusions, such as those of Turkish origin. There are also several frequency variations across Eurasia, influenced by the presence of other haplogroups. For example, M89 (Hg F) is common in Korea and India, M170 (Hg I, particularly I1a and I1c [M223]) originates from Northwestern Europe, and M172 (Hg J2) is associated with the spread of farming from the Near East. From Northeast Asia, M130 (Hg C) is common in Mongolia, while haplotypes such as M124 (Hg R2) show a maximum frequency in Central Asia.
